title: The Aboriginal Issue
subtitle: Victimhood is more corrosive than payments with obligations
contentHtml:
My introduction to Darwin was a bottle fight between two aboriginal men that neither could win, because both were too drunk.

It was in the desolate courtyard of the Northern Territory Supreme Court, an immaculate white building, empty other than still figures scattered in whatever shade there was. Those however were collapsed and quiet, but these two were up and shouting at each other, bottles raised high. They were in the middle of the circular plaza, combatants connected like a game of spinning tops, wobbling towards the middle, armed, and then contact, but with no “bam!”, just the silence of wild swings that sent them stumbling back towards the perimeter, before they regained composure, located each other, and did it all over.

If there had been anyone next to me I would have wagered a bet on who would win, which ended up being the slighter of the two, when his opponent fell backwards, not because he was hit, but from the torque of his own bottle held high, which fell to the ground, shattered, while he collapsed, supine, oblivious to the overhead sun. The other man shambled off towards the shade, shouting insults into the void, to collect what prize I don’t know, certainly not praise, because it was a solitary scene played out only for me and a few inquisitive magpies, who hopped towards the shattered glass, picked at the shards, and then flew off disappointed.

I wasn’t shocked by this at all, didn’t worry for my safety, or theirs, because I’d seen similar scenes last year from Townsville to Alice Springs, where I quickly came to expect public drunkenness and outdoor bar fights rendered comical by the toothlessness and ubiquity of them.

That trip my first memory was seeing an aboriginal man passed out in the middle of a sidewalk, immune to the people stepping over him. This time, when I finally reached Alice Springs after a twenty-two hour bus trip from Darwin, my introduction was running into an aboriginal man on the path from the bus station to my hotel, standing a few yards into the scrub, his shorts around his ankles, pleasuring himself, looking across the dry river bed into the city. He didn’t seem particularly bothered by my presence, although he did pull up his shorts, and gather himself together enough to ask for a few dollars. I thought of pointing out the sign I’d recently passed, the one that said, “This area contains Arrernte sacred sites. (Four Corners Council of Elders)”, and that his behavior was probably sacrilegious, no matter his faith, but I was certain he was too drunk to understand.

Again, this wasn’t surprising, or shocking. Neither of these moments would have been notable, except that they came first, and I could list hundreds of others, because the amount of addiction in the aboriginal community is absolutely absurd. Being in any Australian neighborhoods with a significant aboriginal population means seeing the dysfunction from their addiction, or more commonly, ignoring it, because it’s politically impolite to talk about.

That's not to say every aboriginal is a drunk — sobriety and moderate drinking do exist — but they are something to be celebrated rather than expected.

There is also a different tenor to the dysfunction — it’s largely confined to alcohol abuse, so gone are the tweakers, leaners, and twitchers — and it’s rarely aggressive to outsiders (although domestic abuse is a substantial problem). Almost everyone involved is polite, keeping to themselves, and even when they do approach asking for money it’s with an apologetic tone, giving it almost an “old school charm.” A “Never mind me, I’m just the lovable town drunk” ethos that populates US sitcoms of the past.

Dane, the gentleman whose photo I used two weeks ago is a perfect example of that. I met him in a Darwin McDonald’s, just released from prison, clutching a bag of his possessions, counting his change to see if he had enough for a meal. I offered to buy him one, which he initially declined, before finally accepting, and was parsimonious in his choice, and effusive with the thanks. He didn’t, as I am used to in the US when doing the same, try to “take me deep.” Didn’t order more than he needed, to maybe sell later.

Yet even among the sober aboriginals, few work1, and those who do work mostly in jobs providing social services to their own community — Addiction outreach programs, government bureaucrats and NGO workers handling the heaps of aid funneled into the region. The result is an entire ecosystem built on dysfunction — the highly addicted at the engorged bottom, living to drink; the less so in the middle, shuttling between town binges and bush sobriety; then the functional at the top, providing triage to all the rest.

That money pumped into the communities is enormous — with billions of targeted aid per year and several times that in general public services — simply based on their identity, location, and poverty. There are wildly different accounts of how much each member of the community receives, based on how one chooses to tally it up, what to include and what not to, but also because the resource royalties vary by the precise community they live in. Those royalties are a payment they get from the mining companies2 based on the amount of iron ore, gold, and gases extracted from their ancestral lands, and that depends on which tribe they belong to.

Whatever the amount, and I’ve heard (from them themselves and from critics of the system, so the validity is highly questionable) anywhere from thirty thousand to three hundred thousand per year, it’s substantial enough that few feel the need to earn more.3

That means while the moments of public intoxication are the spectacle, the far more common scene is one of idleness. Of groups of aboriginals clustered without purpose, their movements determined only by the shifting sun, picking up their bags and blankets, as they follow the shade.

That is what is most striking about being around the aboriginals, which is the lack of hustle — the apathy, the purposelessness — of people who seem content to sit all day doing nothing but chatting among themselves. The only time they are activated, when the entrepreneurial impulse kicks in, is when they are unable to drink, either because they blew all their bimonthly check already, or because they have been placed on the banned list.

That is notably different from the other relatively impoverished communities I’ve been in — the slums in Laos, Senegal, Kenya, Uganda, Kyrgyzstan, Indonesia, etc — where people are constantly striving, out and about trying to make it, hawking wares, offering to do any work for any money. I kept being reminded of the gentleman in Dakar who roamed the streets near my hotel with a homemade mobile cart of wood, its sides festooned with giant images of roaches, selling insecticide. There are thousands of them in any African city, selling whatever you need4.

There is little to none of that in the aboriginal communities, where almost all the service jobs are done by temporary workers from those poorer countries. So that you get scene after scene like I saw this year of an Indonesian hustling to serve an aboriginal, to make enough money to ship back home to their family, and to build themselves a career. Or last year, of South Sudanese security guards policing intoxicated aboriginals, a particularly cynical choice by authorities because they believe the optics look better. A black man scolding another black man.

Meanwhile all the “good” high-paying jobs, in mining, agriculture, and what manufacturing there is, is overwhelmingly done by non-aboriginal Australians, including the FIFO’s — those who fly into the outback for a stint, then fly out again. Or as I saw in my bus trip from Darwin, bus far into the empty void, and then bus out again, including a sixteen year old.

While as I have noted many times before I am very sympathetic to the aboriginal community, and fond of their culture, I don’t know how anyone can pretend what is going on in the outback isn’t deeply broken.

A lot of non-aboriginal Australians in the region agree, especially those living close to them, although they keep those views to themselves, unless you ask. It is considered impolite to point out the obvious, for some good reasons and some bad.

J was like that. A sixty-five year old man who has lived in the Northern Territory all his life, working primarily as a long haul driver, and with aboriginals. He is a large gregarious guy, a pat on the back guy, and I watched him dealing with them, and he was as warm and friendly to them as anyone, without an ounce of animosity, but in private he’s harsh, and direct. “They never work now. Never. I been working since I was fourteen, have had to, and never once, even when times were rough, have I taken a hand out. They live off of my taxes, and some of them are bloody rich. Get twenty thousand a month for sitting on their arse. Didn’t used to be that way, when I was a kid they were normal part of the town. They worked like everyone else, we played cricket with them in school, then something changed about twenty years ago. I don’t know what exactly, but they stopped working, their kids stopped going to school, and now they run around with nothing to do but get pissed.”

The children not going to school is indeed an issue, and it’s the reason for the “No school No service” signs you see on almost every shop door, which is clearly an attempt to keep idle aboriginal teens out of stores. A polite, wink-wink-nudge-nudge, way to voice the impolite.

One thing that did change roughly twenty years ago was an increase in the payments to the community, including higher royalty shares, which frustrated residents claim is the primary problem, and provides the answer. Which is to stop handing over money to aboriginals with no strings attached.

While I might agree that forking over cash without any obligations can indeed be corrosive to a culture, making it dependent, promoting idleness, I also believe those payments in this instance are justified. As I’ve argued before, there is a strong case, morally and legally, that the descendants of a population that have lived in Australia for sixty thousand years, who arguably “own the land” deserve a share of the proceeds when the wealth from that land is extracted. Even if not by them. If I find oil on my property, I would, and should, receive a share of the proceeds if I allow a company to drill on it.

I am also sympathetic because of the situation the current aboriginals find themselves in. The culture they come from, that forms their identity and sense of self, of living off the land and their wits, of reverence for the natural world, that existed for sixty thousand years, is about as different from modern life as possible. It’s having to hunt each day to eat, versus walking over to the McDonald’s for the Big Mac meal. As I wrote last year,

Aboriginals for the last two hundred years have faced a close to impossible choice—give up everything about their past, and how they live, to embrace modernity, or continue to live as "primitives," roundly mocked for a way of living that almost everyone else sees as backwards, unable to grasp the deeper, transcendent parts to this way of life. That this choice was often brutally made for them, by force, makes the whole situation far worse, and more complicated.

So what is the solution then? My answer, which isn’t a cop out I promise, is that I don’t believe there is a solution, short of full aboriginal assimilation into modern life, a choice they have to make on their own. You shouldn’t force people who have been there as long as they have, to change, to give up a reverence for their tradition, even if it is “holding them back”. They are not immigrants asking to be citizens — they are as far from that as possible — and have no obligation to conform. It’s akin to demanding a Catholic become a Muslim, but even more substantial than that. Thick culture cannot be changed that way.

What can and should change though is the constant talk of the aboriginals being victims, which is what you hear from academics, politicians, and local leaders, and consequently now, the aboriginals themselves, especially the younger ones. The aboriginal community currently sits in a vacuum, a hole left by having one leg in modernity and another in tradition, and replacing that with victimhood is far more corrosive than payments.

Victimhood is a culture built around the negative, around the dependent, with no pull towards the good. It pollutes the soul, while also perpetuating the belief that you are lesser, needing help, without any agency of your own.

You cannot build an identity around being oppressed, owed, and wronged — even when great injustices were done — because it becomes an anchor that holds everything in place and eventually pulls it under, into nihilism and resignation, completely devoid of any agency. Whatever I do isn’t my fault, so why do anything.

The community is now being properly paid for their land, and if it’s going to move forward, find the right place in the modern world, that needs to be done with pride, dignity, and grace, not with grievance, humiliation, and resentment.

Embracing victimhood is a deadening path to nowhere, and I would argue is as responsible for drunkenness as being paid for doing nothing, because it hollows out a person, replacing volition with vacancy.

The cover photo is of Janet Golder, a member of the Arrernte people, who I met in the Alice Springs casino soon after I sent out a series of blunt tweets about the “aboriginal problem”, which given the medium, was far less nuanced than this essay.

Janet was also not a dysfunctional addict, although she liked to share a beer or two now and then. She is an artist, with works in galleries, and lives in a bush community, but comes to town every few weeks, to have a few drinks while playing the slots, and have McDonald’s.

Meeting her so soon after my tweets was perhaps God's reminder that every “problem group” is composed of individuals with souls, agency, dreams, and pains. That is something I hope I never forget, no matter how frustrated I become. While problems might be statistical, a bothersome blip in a spreadsheet, people are not.

As feel-good an ending as that was, as much as I enjoyed talking to her about life in the bush, about her deep appreciation for the sky, hills, and trees around her traditional home, when I went up to the bar to buy her a second beer, I turned around and there were four of her “uncles and aunts”, standing inches away from me, holding empty mugs, expectant looks on their faces. One of them said, “you buy for her, you buy for us as well?” and I said no, no I won’t and then my evening was over because I was the mark, the guy in the bar that they felt owed them.

I thought then of what another aboriginal man, Edgar, told me last year. He had none of the dysfunction I've described above, was well-adjusted, happy, and doing OK, with a law career. He was the assimilated aboriginal, balancing the modern and the traditional. When I’d mentioned having been pestered a few times by locals asking for drinks he said how frustrated he was by that, because “we were raised never to ask an outsider for help. You turn to your family, not a stranger.”

When I asked him why they were now doing that, he said, “Because it’s all gone to shiite.”

(Prior pieces on Australia: First impressions of Sydney, Sydney the suburban paradise, Twenty-seven hours on the Aussie dog, Alice Springs, Final thoughts on Australia, Perth, What makes Australia Australia?, Riding the Aussie Dog. Again)

PS: I will be home for the remainder of the month, then I have a long trip to Asia. The tentative schedule is as follows.

  • Seoul: Oct 8th - 15th

  • Manila: 16th - 22nd

  • Kuala Lumpur: 22nd - 27th

  • Yangon (Myanmar): 27th - 31st

  • Guangzhou/Hong Kong: Nov 1st - 4th

  • Okinawa, and surrounding islands: 5th - 16th (I will be taking ferries from Naha to Kagoshima)

As usual, if you happen to be in any of those locations then, please reach out to me.

1

In the 2021 Census, among Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in the Northern Territory, only 33.5% were in the labor force. It drops from that in what is labeled very remote locations.

2

They are not direct payments to the individuals from the companies, but rather payments that go into a fund, that are then distributed based on tribal affiliation. It’s a pedantic point, but this issue brings out the pedants.

3

There is a lot of disagreement on the numbers involved, but in 2015–16, total government expenditure on services to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Australians was estimated at $33.4 billion. About 82% of that is considered mainstream government expenditure. Per person, that comes out to be about twice that of non-Indigenous Australians, although the argument is made that the bulk of the difference is because of the remoteness of the communities, which seems like a distraction, because living remote is what Aboriginals do.

4

The amount of hustle in any African city is impressive. Whatever else the stereotypes are, they are not lazy. Not by any stretch.
